sentences.text: She went to the chapel wall at first light and the hollow was empty and there was frost on the stones.
She stood there for a while in the cold doing the only useful thing available, which was working out precisely what she had lost.
It was not that Emese would read it.
Nobody reads them.
She knew that, she had always known that, and she made herself say it out loud on the road to be sure she believed it: *nobody is going to read it.* What she had lost was the sentence.
She had put down, three days early, in a temper, the true and specific thing that would have ended it — and it had gone, and it was not available to her any more.
She could remember writing it.
She could not, standing at that wall in the frost, actually get hold of the sentence.
It had the shape of a word you cannot find, and it stayed like that for the rest of her life, and she has never once been able to reconstruct it.
Which left her with the other thing.
The small one.
The one about the voice at the shop.
She said it to Emese on the Saturday, at the bus stop, badly, in about four sentences, looking at the timetable and not at Emese.
Emese was baffled, and apologised, and meant it, and did not understand.
And then, about a week later, said — out of nowhere, in the middle of something else entirely — "I do do that.
The thing you said.
I did it to Réka on Tuesday and I heard myself." They are thirty-one now.
Emese lives in Budapest and Bori does not, and they speak most weeks, and they have had one serious falling-out in the whole of that time and it was about something else.
Bori has put a letter out every October since she was fifteen.

She has never once written in a temper again — she writes hers in the first week of the month now, in daylight, at the kitchen table, and takes several days over it — and she has never gone out to retrieve one, and she has never told anybody in her family what is in them.
She has thought a great deal about what her grandmother said, and she has an addition to it that she has not said to anybody either.
Her grandmother said it was a place to put a thing.
Bori thinks it is also a way of finding out which thing was the real one.
You can only put out one.

You sit down with everything you have been carrying, and you have to choose, and the choosing is the whole of it — because whatever you write down is going away for good, and whatever you do not write down is the thing you are going to have to say out loud to somebody at a bus stop.
